query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled volume fraction of high-quality graphene into the W–Cu composite will enhance interfacial thermal conduction, thereby increasing overall thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance compared to the conventional composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard W–Cu metal-matrix composite with no graphene reinforcement.
generation.intervention: Introduce 1–5 vol% graphene reinforcement during composite processing to form graphene bridges between the tungsten and copper phases.
generation.conditions: High-temperature operational environments and neutron irradiation conditions typical of heat-dissipation and fusion reactor joint applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Graphene reinforcement at the tungsten–copper interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The high in-plane thermal conductivity of graphene provides efficient thermal bridges at the phase boundaries, facilitating heat transfer across the composite without compromising the mechanical interlocking or irradiation tolerance of the matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in the composite's thermal conductivity relative to the baseline, while maintaining comparable mechanical durability and resistance to irradiation-induced damage.
generation.baseline: A conventional W–Cu composite processed without graphene reinforcement.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold when the graphene content is optimized (within 1–5 vol%) and uniformly dispersed; too high a concentration or poor dispersion might diminish mechanical durability or induce processing defects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of thermal conductivity improvement and its trade-offs under all operating conditions remain uncertain, as processing variations and graphene dispersion quality may influence the final properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composites under identical processing conditions: one set with 1–5 vol% graphene reinforcement and one control set without graphene. Subject both sets to standardized thermal cycling and irradiation exposure reflective of fusion-reactor conditions.
measurements: Quantitative thermal conductivity measurements over the operational temperature range.
Mechanical durability testing (e.g., tensile and fatigue tests).
Irradiation resistance assessments (e.g., microstructural analysis post-irradiation).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the graphene-reinforced composites do not show a statistically significant increase in thermal conductivity compared to the control or exhibit a corresponding decline in mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.approach: Incorporate graphene reinforcement to boost interfacial thermal conductivity
